title: What is the Spark / PySpark DataFrame programming model — transformations (`select`, `filter`, `withColumn`, `join`) are lazy and only build a plan, while actions (`show`, `collect`, `count`, `write`) trigger execution — and how does a PySpark DataFrame differ from a Pandas DataFrame (distributed across a cluster + lazy vs single-machine in-memory + eager), including null handling (`dropna`, `fillna` / `when`-`otherwise`)?
shortTitle: The Spark / PySpark DataFrame programming model (vs Pandas)

s1_definition.profdef: A Spark DataFrame is a distributed, immutable, lazily-evaluated table of rows partitioned across a cluster. Transformations such as `select`, `filter`, `withColumn`, and `join` are lazy and only build a logical plan, while actions such as `show`, `collect`, `count`, and `write` trigger the Catalyst optimizer to compile and execute that plan. A Pandas DataFrame, by contrast, is a single-machine, in-memory, eagerly-evaluated table that executes each operation immediately and is limited by one machine's RAM.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of analysing the National Bank of India's transactions. A Pandas DataFrame is like one accountant with one desk: every instruction you give is done right now, but the whole ledger must fit on that one desk, so a billion rows will not fit. A Spark DataFrame is like a huge team of accountants across many desks (the cluster). When you say "filter positive amounts, then total by account", the team does not start yet — a manager writes down the whole plan first (lazy). Only when you finally say "show me the result" (an action) does the manager optimize the plan and send the team to work in parallel. Lazy planning plus many desks is what lets Spark handle data far too big for any single machine.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spark DataFrames are distributed and lazy, building an optimized plan that only runs on an action; Pandas DataFrames are single-machine and eager, running every step immediately.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Spark DataFrame is a distributed, immutable, lazily-evaluated table of rows partitioned across a cluster. Transformations such as `select`, `filter`, `withColumn`, and `join` are lazy and only build a logical plan, while actions such as `show`, `collect`, `count`, and `write` trigger the Catalyst optimizer to compile and execute that plan. A Pandas DataFrame, by contrast, is a single-machine, in-memory, eagerly-evaluated table that executes each operation immediately and is limited by one machine's RAM.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of analysing the National Bank of India's transactions. A Pandas DataFrame is like one accountant with one desk: every instruction you give is done right now, but the whole ledger must fit on that one desk, so a billion rows will not fit. A Spark DataFrame is like a huge team of accountants across many desks (the cluster). When you say "filter positive amounts, then total by account", the team does not start yet — a manager writes down the whole plan first (lazy). Only when you finally say "show me the result" (an action) does the manager optimize the plan and send the team to work in parallel. Lazy planning plus many desks is what lets Spark handle data far too big for any single machine.

**One line to remember:** Spark DataFrames are distributed and lazy, building an optimized plan that only runs on an action; Pandas DataFrames are single-machine and eager, running every step immediately.

sections.s2_technical:
The heart of the model is lazy evaluation. When you call a transformation, Spark does not compute anything; it records the operation into a logical plan. `df.filter(df.amount > 0)` returns a new DataFrame describing "the original with a filter", not the filtered rows. You can chain many transformations — `df.filter(...).select(...).withColumn(...).join(other, "accountId")` — and still nothing has run. This laziness is powerful because Spark's Catalyst optimizer can see the whole chain and optimize it as a unit: it pushes filters down to the source, prunes unused columns, and reorders joins before any data moves.

Execution only happens when you call an action. Actions are operations that need a concrete result: `count()` returns a number, `collect()` pulls rows to the driver, `show()` prints a sample, and `write()` persists output. At that moment Catalyst compiles the logical plan into an optimized physical plan and runs it across the cluster. A crucial practical consequence is that each action re-runs the plan from the start unless you `cache()` or `persist()` an intermediate DataFrame, so a senior engineer caches a DataFrame that multiple actions reuse to avoid recomputation.

The DataFrame is distributed and immutable. The rows are split into partitions spread across executors, so operations run in parallel, and transformations never mutate a DataFrame; they return a new one. Wide transformations like `join` and `groupBy` require a shuffle, moving data across the network to co-locate matching keys, which is the expensive part to minimize, whereas narrow transformations like `filter` and `select` need no shuffle.

The contrast with Pandas is fundamental. Pandas is single-machine, in-memory, and eager: every call executes immediately and the entire DataFrame must fit in one machine's RAM, which is perfect for datasets up to a few gigabytes and interactive exploration but cannot scale to a billion rows. PySpark distributes across a cluster and defers execution, scaling to terabytes but adding cluster overhead that makes it slower for tiny data. Null handling exists in both but with Spark's API: `df.na.drop()` or `df.dropna()` removes rows with nulls, `df.na.fill(0)` or `df.fillna({"amount": 0})` replaces them, and conditional logic uses `when`/`otherwise`, for example `df.withColumn("status", when(col("balance") < 0, "OVERDRAWN").otherwise("OK"))` which labels each account. A senior nuance is that PySpark offers a Pandas-compatible API and Arrow-based conversion, so teams can prototype in Pandas and scale the same logic in Spark, and the right choice is Pandas for small interactive work and Spark when data outgrows one machine. In a bank, exploratory analysis of a sample might use Pandas, but production jobs over the full transaction history use Spark DataFrames.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank chains several operations on transactions, and we want them optimized together and run only once. This is exactly lazy transformations plus an action — build a plan, then execute.

Problem 2 — Raw data has nulls that must be dropped or filled before aggregation. This is exactly Spark null handling with dropna and fillna.

Problem 3 — We must label each account's status conditionally. This is exactly when/otherwise.

Because a real Spark cluster is heavy, the mini-project simulates the DataFrame model in Java. `MiniDataFrame` records lazy transformations (`filter`, `withColumnStatus`, `fillNaAmount`) into a plan and only executes on an action (`collect`, `count`). It processes in-memory rows to mimic the behaviour, printing when the plan is built versus executed. The demo builds a chained plan with null handling and conditional labelling, then triggers it with an action.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four rows: Rajesh 1200, Priya 150000, Rajesh with a null amount, and Priya with a negative -50.

Step 1 — Build the plan. Three transformations are chained: fill null amounts with zero, filter to keep non-negative amounts, and add a status column using when/otherwise. Each call only records a step into the plan; the logs confirm nothing has executed yet. This is lazy evaluation.

Step 2 — Trigger with an action. Calling collect is an action, so now the plan runs. Spark-style, the source rows are copied first to preserve immutability, then each plan step is applied in order to the copy.

Step 3 — Fillna. The null-amount Rajesh row has its amount replaced with zero, so it now has a concrete value and will not break later arithmetic.

Step 4 — Filter. The negative -50 Priya row is dropped because it is below zero. The zero-amount Rajesh row survives because the filter keeps non-negative values. Three rows remain.

Step 5 — Conditional status and output. The when/otherwise step labels each surviving row: Priya's 150000 becomes HIGH_VALUE, while Rajesh's 1200 and 0 become NORMAL. The action returns the final rows, and a second action, count, re-runs the plan and returns three. The chained lazy plan executed exactly when the action demanded a result.

```
INFO: === Build lazy plan (no execution yet) ===
INFO: plan += fillNaAmount (LAZY)
INFO: plan += filter (LAZY, not executed)
INFO: plan += withColumn(status) via when/otherwise (LAZY)
INFO: Plan built. Still nothing executed.
INFO: === Trigger with an ACTION ===
INFO: ACTION collect(): optimizing + executing the plan
INFO: SAV2001 amount=1200 status=NORMAL
INFO: CUR3001 amount=150000 status=HIGH_VALUE
INFO: SAV2001 amount=0 status=NORMAL
INFO: ACTION count(): executing the plan
INFO: count() = 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  4 rows (incl null amount + negative)
    │ TRANSFORMATIONS (lazy — build plan only)
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Logical Plan                                   │
  │  1. fillNaAmount(0)                            │
  │  2. filter(amount >= 0)                        │
  │  3. withColumn(status via when/otherwise)      │
  └───────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ ACTION (collect/count) → Catalyst optimizes + runs
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Execution across partitions                    │
  │  null→0 | drop -50 | label HIGH_VALUE/NORMAL  │
  └───────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                  ▼
  SAV2001 1200 NORMAL | CUR3001 150000 HIGH_VALUE | SAV2001 0 NORMAL
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Spark DataFrame is a distributed, immutable, lazily-evaluated table of rows spread across a cluster. The heart of the model is laziness: transformations like select, filter, withColumn, and join do not compute anything, they only record operations into a logical plan, so I can chain many of them and still nothing has run. Execution happens only when I call an action like count, collect, show, or write, and at that moment Spark's Catalyst optimizer sees the whole chain, pushes filters down, prunes unused columns, and reorders joins before any data moves. One practical consequence I always mention is that each action re-runs the plan from the start, so I cache or persist a DataFrame that several actions reuse to avoid recomputation. Because the DataFrame is distributed and immutable, operations run in parallel over partitions and always return a new DataFrame, and the expensive operations to minimize are wide transformations like join and groupBy that require a shuffle across the network.

The contrast with Pandas is fundamental. Pandas is single-machine, in-memory, and eager, so every call runs immediately and the whole dataset must fit in one machine's RAM, which is ideal for a few gigabytes and interactive exploration but cannot scale to a billion rows. PySpark distributes across a cluster and defers execution, scaling to terabytes at the cost of cluster overhead that makes it slower on tiny data. For nulls, Spark uses dropna to remove rows with nulls, fillna to replace them, and when with otherwise for conditional columns, for example labelling an account overdrawn when the balance is negative and ok otherwise.

In my project at the National Bank of India this shaped how we worked. For quick exploratory analysis on a sample we used Pandas on one machine, but every production job over the full transaction history used Spark DataFrames. A typical job chained fillna to replace missing amounts, a filter to drop invalid rows, and a when/otherwise to flag high-value transactions, and because those transformations were lazy, Spark optimized the entire chain and only executed it when we finally wrote the result or counted the rows. That lazy, distributed model is exactly what let us run the same logical pipeline on terabytes that would never have fit on a single Pandas machine.
